Hip
HIP
n. (the projecting part of the body at the joint of the thigh)
From Old English hype, the hip or haunch, a common Germanic word. In the phrase hip and thigh it became a proverb for utter, unsparing overthrow.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

After the Philistines burned his wife and her father with fire, Samson took vengeance on them: “And he smote them hip and thigh with a great slaughter: and he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam.” The phrase pictures a fighter overthrowing his enemies so completely that limb is heaped upon limb, and it passed from this verse into English as a byword for total defeat. Samson's story is a strange mixture: a Nazarite from the womb, raised up to begin to deliver Israel (Judges 13:5), yet driven again and again by his own appetites and grievances. Here his personal revenge is nonetheless the instrument by which God strikes the Philistine oppressors, for the LORD “sought an occasion against the Philistines” (Judges 14:4). The Spirit of the LORD came upon him in power; his life was not thereby made a pattern of holiness. Hebrews numbers him among those who through faith “out of weakness were made strong” (Hebrews 11:32-34), a reminder that God's deliverances are His own work, done through flawed instruments, and point forward to the one Deliverer whose victory over His enemies is complete and whose life is without sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): HIP, the projecting part of an animal formed by the os ilium or haunch bone; the haunch. To have on the hip, to have the advantage over one.

HIP, n. The projecting part of an animal formed by the os ilium or haunch bone; the haunch, or the flesh that covers the bone and the adjacent parts.

To smite hip and thigh, to overthrow completely; a phrase from Judges 15:8.

To have on the hip, to have the advantage over one.

Judges 15:8 records Samson smiting the Philistines hip and thigh with a great slaughter.

He then dwelt in the top of the rock Etam.

Key Scripture

Jdg 15:8 — "And he smote them hip and thigh with a great slaughter: and he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam."

Jdg 14:4 — "But his father and his mother knew not that it was of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines: for at that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel."

Heb 11:32 — "And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:"

Modern Corruption

Samson is either sentimentalized as a simple hero or dismissed as a mere brute; both readings miss God's sovereign use of a flawed deliverer.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase hip and thigh survives as an idiom for complete overthrow.

The danger lies in how Samson is read. Children's-book heroism forgets his lusts and his ruin; cynical readings forget that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him and that Hebrews counts him among the faithful. Scripture holds both: God sovereignly uses weak and sinful men, and their sins still bring their own bitter harvest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English hype, the haunch; Judges 15:8 gives English the phrase hip and thigh for complete overthrow.

Old English hype, the hip or haunch.

Hebrews 11:32 counts Samson among the faithful.
